Cohen, and Matthew R.V. Ross October 21, 2026 Overview Water clarity is one of our oldest and most intuitive lenses into aquatic ecosystems. For more than a century, hydrologists and limnologists have lowered Secchi disks into rivers, lakes, and estuaries to measure how deeply light penetrates the water column. Yet Secchi disk depth (\(z_{SD}\), in meters) alone tells us only how much light is lost—not what is blocking it. Across inland and coastal waters, diffuse light attenuation (\(k_d = 1 / z_{SD}\); Lee et al. 2015) is governed by pure water (\(k_w\)) and three primary light-attenuating constituents (LACs): non-algal particles (NAP), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and phytoplankton chlorophyll a (\(\text{Chl }a\)). Under the additive Beer–Lambert model, Secchi depth can be written directly in terms of constituent concentrations: \[z_{SD} = \frac{1}{k_w + \alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a}\] To understand how these three constituents partition water clarity across the contiguous United States, we built an open-source pipeline on top of the AquaMatch data suite (Brousil et al. 2024a, 2024b, 2025; De La Torre et al. 2025)—the successor to AquaSat (Ross et al. 2019). Combining 277,382 simultaneous four-variable matchups (Secchi + Chl a + DOC + TSS/SSC) for model calibration with 478,929 three-constituent matchups across 39,396 monitoring stations (1970–2025), we estimate regional specific attenuation coefficients (\(\alpha_i\)) across U.S. EPA Level III ecoregions and project nearly half a million water quality observations into ternary attenuation space. Why Optical Partitioning & Total Visibility Both Matter ({sonicray} 3D Simulation) Ternary diagrams are a powerful way to visualize which constituent dominates light attenuation (\(f_{\text{NAP}} + f_{\text{DOC}} + f_{\text{Chl }a} = 1\)), but proportions alone miss a critical physical dimension: total visibility (\(z_{SD}\)). Two lakes sitting at the exact same coordinate in ternary space can represent either a crystal-clear oligotrophic basin (\(z_{SD} > 5\text{ m}\)) or a murky waterbody (\(z_{SD} < 0.4\text{ m}\)) when total constituent concentrations scale up. Moreover, each constituent alters the underwater light field in a distinct way: Chlorophyll a (Algae): Absorbs blue and red light while cells scatter green wavelengths, shifting water from deep blue to emerald green. DOC (Brownification): Absorbs short wavelengths exponentially with negligible particulate scattering, turning water into dark tea-stained blackwater. NAP / TSS (Sediment): Strongly backscatters broadband light, turning water chalky tan/ochre and driving the steepest collapse in Secchi visibility. To visualize both ternary composition and total visibility simultaneously, we path-traced a naturalistic 3-hill lake basin on an Apple Silicon Metal GPU using {sonicray}’s native dielectric and Beer–Lambert water engine (sr_upload_mesh(water = ...) + sr_water_preset()). Section 2 Simultaneous Matchups & Initial Hygiene (prep.R) To partition light attenuation among phytoplankton, non-algal particles, and dissolved organic carbon, we need field samples where chl_a, doc, and tss were collected on the same day at the same station (MonitoringLocationIdentifier and date)—which we refer to as matchups. Calibrating our bio-optical model additionally requires a same-day Secchi disk depth (secchi) measurement. am <- get_aquamatch() # 490,209 joined 3-LAC records (1970–2025) simul <- build_simultaneous(am, require_secchi = TRUE) no_secchi <- build_simultaneous(am, require_secchi = FALSE) 2.1 Four Initial Hygiene Filters Before statistical screening, build_simultaneous() in R/prep.R applies four simple, deterministic hygiene rules: Ambient water bodies only: Excludes industrial/municipal Facility outflows, retaining Estuary, Lake, and Stream sites. True Secchi measurements (for 4-variable calibration): Requires sdd_approx == 0 (excluding turbidity tubes) and sdd_mdl <= 1 (excluding \(\le 0.01\text{ m}\) floor placeholders). Same-day deduplication: Collapses duplicate agency uploads of the same bottle sample (distinct(SiteID, date, secchi, chl_a, doc, tss)). Section 3 Separating Non-Algal Particles (NAP) from Bulk TSS Our additive Beer–Lambert model partitions non-water light attenuation among three mutually exclusive pools: phytoplankton (Chl a), non-algal suspended particles (NAP: mineral sediment and detritus), and dissolved organic matter (DOC). Because standard gravimetric filtration measures bulk Total Suspended Solids (TSS)—which captures both mineral sediment and living algal cells on the filter—we subtract living phytoplankton dry mass from bulk TSS before fitting the model: Optical Component Field Measurement Model Predictor & Units Phytoplankton (\(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\,\text{Chl }a\)) Chlorophyll a (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\text{mg m}^{-3} = \mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) used directly Non-algal particles (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\,\text{NAP}\)) Bulk TSS / SSC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - \text{biomass}(\text{Chl }a)\) (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) Dissolved organic matter (\(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\,\text{DOC}\)) DOC (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) \(\text{DOC}\) (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) used directly Following Gohin et al. (2005), we estimate phytoplankton dry biomass (\(\text{mg L}^{-1}\)) from \(\text{Chl }a\) (\(\mu\text{g L}^{-1}\)) as a power law that accounts for intracellular photoacclimation (lower carbon-to-chlorophyll ratios in nutrient-rich blooms; Geider et al. 1997; Cloern et al. 1995): \[\text{biomass}_{\text{algal}}\ [\text{mg L}^{-1}] = 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}, \qquad \text{NAP} = \text{TSS} - 0.234\,(\text{Chl }a)^{0.57}\] Figure 3.1: (a) Empirical TSS vs. Chl a across matchups overlaid with the nonlinear Gohin et al. (2005) algal biomass curve (solid black) and constant linear dry-mass:Chl a ratios (dashed). Section 4 Analytical Floors & Beer–Lambert Plausibility Screening Even after parameter and unit harmonization, roughly 1–2% of multi-agency WQP records contain field-recording anomalies that can heavily leverage ordinary least squares (OLS) slopes. However, simple marginal quantile trimming (clipping the top and bottom 0.1% or 1% of each variable independently) throws away genuine oligotrophic alpine lakes (Secchi up to 13.96 m) and real storm-flow sediment plumes (TSS up to 978 mg/L) while missing joint physical contradictions in the middle of the distribution. To clean recording errors without truncating real extremes or introducing statistical circularity, R/prep.R uses a two-stage protocol (n = 277,382): 4.1 Stage 1: Analytical Reporting Floors (trim_simultaneous()) Rather than dropping low-concentration tails, entries reported below standard EPA/USGS Method Detection Limits (MDLs) are floored via ifelse(x < floor, floor, x) (chl_a = 0.10 µg/L, doc = 0.25 mg/L, tss = 0.50 mg/L, secchi = 0.01 m), retaining 100% of the 281,439 simultaneous 4-variable matchups: Variable Analytical Floor (MDL) Median 99.9th Percentile Maximum Retained Chlorophyll a (µg/L) 0.10 7.33 323.000 990.290 Dissolved Organic Carbon (mg/L) 0.25 6.20 48.000 49.985 Total Suspended Solids / SSC (mg/L) 0.50 8.50 340.000 978.000 Secchi Disk Depth (m) 0.01 0.80 7.687 14.330 4.2 Stage 2: A Priori Beer–Lambert Plausibility Screen (clean_wqp_discordance()) What kinds of errors survive marginal inspection? Two classic WQP artifacts stand out in Figure 4.1a: Unflagged streambed bottom hits (3,157 records, 1.12%): Field crews lower a Secchi disk in a crystal-clear, shallow stream (\(0.05\text{–}0.20\text{ m}\) deep) where the disk hits the gravel bed while still clearly visible, and record the water depth (Secchi = 0.05–0.20 m, implying \(k_d = 5\text{–}20\text{ m}^{-1}\)) without flagging a bottom hit—even though paired bottle chemistry shows ultra-clear water (\(\text{TSS} < 3\text{ mg L}^{-1}\), \(\text{DOC} < 3\text{ mg L}^{-1}\)). Unit and bottle mismatches (900 records, 0.32%): Records reporting clear water (Secchi = 3–10 m) alongside extreme sediment or carbon (\(\text{TSS} > 100\text{ mg L}^{-1}\)), caused by Secchi depth entered in feet rather than meters or storm-flow sediment samples matched to baseflow clarity readings. To screen out these physically contradictory combinations without using our fitted regression models, we compare measured diffuse attenuation (\(k_d = 1 / z_{SD}\)) against a priori Beer–Lambert attenuation (\(k_{d,\text{lit}}\)) calculated strictly from published optical cross-sections (Kirk 1994; Morris et al. 1995; Bannister 1974; Gohin et al. 2005): \[k_{d,\text{lit}} = 0.080 + 0.040\,\max(0, \text{NAP}) + 0.070\,\text{DOC} + 0.016\,\text{Chl }a\] Matchups where observed \(k_d\) and literature \(k_{d,\text{lit}}\) diverge by more than a factor of \(10^{0.80} \approx 6.3\times\) (\(|\log_{10}(k_d / k_{d,\text{lit}})| > 0.80\)) are removed (4,057 rows = 1.44%), leaving 277,382 physically consistent training matchups: Figure 4.1: (a) Observed diffuse attenuation (kd = 1/z_SD) vs. a priori Beer–Lambert expectation (kd,lit) across all 281,439 matchups, highlighting shallow streambed bottom hits (red horizontal bands at Secchi = 0.05–0.20 m) and unit/bottle mismatches (blue). Section 5 Hierarchical Ecoregion Stratification (ecoregions.R) A gram of dissolved organic carbon or suspended sediment does not attenuate the exact same amount of light everywhere. Humic DOC drained from northern peatlands is darker and more aromatic than autochthonous DOC in arid reservoirs (Spencer et al. 2012; Griffin et al. 2018), and fine clay suspensions scatter light much more efficiently per unit mass than coarse glacial silt (Bowers et al. 2020). To capture this regional biogeochemical coherence across streams, lakes, and estuaries within a single continental framework, eco_join() in R/ecoregions.R assigns each monitoring station (SiteID) to its nested U.S. EPA / CEC North American Ecoregion across Levels I–IV (Omernik & Griffith 2014). Nearshore estuarine stations located slightly seaward of coastline polygons are matched to the nearest coastal ecoregion via sf::st_nearest_feature(), guaranteeing a strict 1-to-1 mapping from SiteID to ecoregion. Section 6 Hierarchical Bio-Optical Models (models.R) 6.1 Additive Beer–Lambert Model Formulation We test ten candidate linear models that estimate specific light-attenuation coefficients (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}, \alpha_{\text{DOC}}, \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\)) via ordinary least squares (OLS) with a fixed pure-water attenuation offset \(k_w = 0.04776\text{ m}^{-1}\) and no intercept: \[k_d - k_w = \alpha_{\text{NAP},g}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC},g}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a,g}\,\text{Chl }a, \qquad z_{SD} = \frac{1}{k_w + \alpha_{\text{NAP},g}\,\text{NAP} + \alpha_{\text{DOC},g}\,\text{DOC} + \alpha_{\text{Chl }a,g}\,\text{Chl }a}\] Here \(g\) indexes the stratification group: continental USA (Model 1), water-body type alone (Model 2), EPA Ecoregion Levels I–IV without water-type separation (Models 3, 5, 7, 9), or EPA Ecoregion Levels I–IV crossed with water-body type (Models 4, 6, 8, 10). Section 7 Coefficient Stability & Sample-Size Convergence (Fig. S1) Do regional differences in fitted attenuation slopes (\(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}, \alpha_{\text{DOC}}, \alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\)) reflect real biogeochemical differences across ecoregions, or just small-sample estimation noise? To answer this, we randomly partition the 277,382 training matchups into \(G\) subsets of varying sample size (\(n/50, n/100, \dots, n/10{,}000\), plus \(G=1\)) and refit the three-constituent model across 10 independent Monte Carlo replicates (random_subset_coefs() in R/models.R, seed P$random_seed = 20240826). Figure 7.1: Figure S1: Coefficient coherence cones across sample sizes. Grey ribbons span the 0.001%–99.999% quantiles of slopes fitted to random subsets of size n across all data and by water-body type. Colored circles mark Level III ecoregion fits (Models 7 and 8). Once group sample size exceeds \(n \approx 1{,}000\), random sampling variability narrows into a tight cone around the continental mean (grey ribbon). Regional estimates of \(\alpha_{\text{Chl }a}\) (chl_a, top row) stay tightly clustered inside the random-sampling cone, whereas ecoregion-specific slopes for \(\alpha_{\text{DOC}}\) (doc, middle row) and \(\alpha_{\text{NAP}}\) (tss_dead, bottom row) spread well outside the random-sampling envelope even at \(n > 10{,}000\). That spread reflects genuine regional differences in dissolved organic matter aromaticity (Spencer et al. 2012; Griffin et al. 2018) and suspended particle size and mineralogy (Dodds & Whiles 2004; Gohin et al. 2005).
